misconceptions.claim: A replicated production site eliminates disaster-recovery planning.
misconceptions.correction: Replication can copy corruption, rely on unavailable dependencies, or fail under regional, provider, identity, or human disruption.

misconceptions.claim: The fastest restore is always the best recovery.
misconceptions.correction: The source must be trustworthy and the recovered service must meet security, integrity, dependency, and business acceptance criteria.

outcome: Given a service disruption, choose a recovery strategy that matches business impact and recovery objectives, identify dependencies and alternate capabilities, and define how trust and service acceptance will be restored.

sections.body: A recovery strategy translates business priorities and impact analysis into capabilities such as redundancy, high availability, fault tolerance, backups, alternate processing sites, manual workarounds, reciprocal arrangements, or cloud recovery. Recovery time objective, recovery point objective, maximum tolerable downtime, service dependencies, data integrity, staffing, communications, and cost shape the choice. A strategy should state what is protected, how the service fails over or is rebuilt, and who accepts the recovered service.
keyPoints: RTO concerns how quickly service returns; RPO concerns the acceptable data-loss point; MTD expresses business tolerance.
High availability and fault tolerance reduce interruption but do not guarantee clean recovery from corruption or compromise.
Dependencies, people, data, facilities, suppliers, and communications can be recovery bottlenecks.
sections.title: Match strategy to business need

sections.body: Recovery must address integrity and security as well as availability. Protect backups and recovery images, establish clean sources, verify dependencies and configuration, control emergency access, validate data and monitoring, and obtain business and security acceptance before normal operation. Record decisions, timing, deviations, and residual risk, and feed lessons into continuity, architecture, and operational plans.
keyPoints: A fast restore from a compromised source can reintroduce the incident.
Recovery acceptance needs technical, security, and business criteria.
Recovery capabilities require maintenance, testing, staff readiness, and supplier commitments.
sections.title: Restore a trustworthy service

summary: Recovery strategies define how an organization maintains or restores critical services after disruption. They balance business priorities, dependencies, recovery objectives, resilience, alternate processing, backups, communications, people, and trustworthy return to operation.

assumptions: The scenario is a bounded application of the canonical unit, not a universal threshold, legal conclusion, or vendor prescription.
Directed edges carry only their printed relation; proximity and shared color do not imply ownership, authorization, or chronology.
Acceptance applies only to the stated scope and retained evidence; unknown or excluded conditions remain explicit.

learningJob.plainExplanation: RTO describes return time, RPO the acceptable data-loss point, and MTD the business tolerance. A recovery strategy must include trust, people, network, key, capacity, communication, and acceptance dependencies rather than alternate compute alone.
learningJob.visualReasoningGain: A dependency-and-time comparison would show why compute plus data does not satisfy RTO/RPO when identity, keys, network, and acceptance are absent; the opening does not.
